title: Heckling squad: how they got to Vienna and bad quarters
summary: The band hooked on with the New York delegation, got poor lodging and faced riots, and stayed apolitical, calling communists 'Indians' and others 'cowboys'.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, over there, who sent these groups, uh, from America?

Well, uh, you have a, a large communist following in New York. And you have a large communist following in Chicago, you see. So, uh, what happened, we were able to latch on with one of the, uh, two big groups, like I said, which was New York and Chicago. We were able to latch on with the, uh, the New York group. We went over with them, see. And, uh, well, like I say, this thing being in a free country, I mean, they couldn't very well put us out, you see. So, uh, we got over there and, uh, we were, we were the official heckling squad.
Did the, uh, communists provide you places to play value over there?

Uh, well, uh, what happened, uh, the living quarters we had and the accommodations were terrible. I mean, none of us, uh, you know, were too happy over the setup over there. But, uh, we figured if we could stick it out for, for ten days, we got it with, see. Now, I think they arranged these bad plays as far as with the intentions of us getting fed up and leaving, you see. That's what they, they couldn't very well tell us to get out, but they didn't want us to stay, you see. So, when they seen that that wouldn't work, uh, well, they, they just about put us under all kind of conditions you could think of like that, say. But when they seen that wouldn't work, then they resorted to violence. I mean, they were having street fights and riots, you know, all the time. Uh, but none of this affected the band in any way because we went over strictly as musicians, not as a political group. You see, we had no connections with the, with politics whatsoever, you see. And, uh, half of the time, uh, the communists and the non-communists hardly knew which side we were on, you see. I mean, they just came for the sake of listening to the music, you know. And the last few days of the festival, of course, they found out that, you know, we were, we were non-communish, you know. But, uh, the way we refer to them, uh, we call the communist Indians and the non-communist the cowboys. And whenever we would talk within the band, you know, we, we'd refer to them as the cowboys and Indians. So, if there was any bad guys listening, they didn't know what was going on, you see. And it worked, though. It was the cowboys and the Indians. That's funny. You see, we, we didn't want to get involved in politics in any way, you see. We didn't go over there for political purposes. We went over to play music and to have the prestigious same we played in Europe, you see. And, uh, I mean, it's a great thing, you know. It's not every, everybody gets a chance to go to Europe and play music, you know.
Well, jazz is a little bigger than all that jazz. Yeah.
You know, anyway. Well, I tell you, I never thought I would ever travel around the world on a stage. I mean, I got to go to Cuba, went to Europe, all on the oil horn. Mobile, they say no.
Been to slide down yet? No, uh, they tell me we're going to play at the snake farm next week.
Well, you had to learn some special numbers like that. Snake rag.
Louis Armstrong did it. Yeah. Well, uh, anyway.
